title: Birth
full_review:
In giving birth to "Birth" (New Line), a metaphysical love story about a woman who comes to believe that her dead husband has been reincarnated as a 10-year-old boy, British director Jonathan Glazer had to endure his fair share of labor pains, including choruses of boos at festival screenings and a minifirestorm ignited by one of the film's more controversial scenes.

Still, controversy notwithstanding, Glazer has managed to craft an elegiac meditation on love, loss and mortality, buttressed by exceptional performances from the assembled ensemble, hauntingly evocative visuals, deliberate pacing and a disquietingly plaintive score.

Sporting a pixie haircut reminiscent of Mia Farrow's close-cropped coif in "Rosemary's Baby," Nicole Kidman stars as Anna, a 35-year-old New York widow, still grieving the death of her husband, Sean, who dropped dead while jogging through a snow-blanketed Central Park 10 years earlier. The episode, which plays out during the film's opening credits, is one of the movie's most visually arresting sequences.

Trying to move on, she accepts a marriage proposal from Joseph (Danny Huston), a genial businessman who understands her emotional fragility.

During a birthday celebration at her mother's (Lauren Bacall) tony Upper East Side apartment, an intense young boy also named Sean (Cameron Bright) slips in from the downstairs lobby just in time to interrupt the cake-cutting with a request to speak to Anna in private. Once alone, he tells her that he is actually her late husband, and voices adamant disapproval of her plans to remarry.
Shaken, Anna shrugs it off as a hurtful prank and escorts him out. Not easily dissuaded, Sean continues to contact Anna, writing her letters, despite cease-and-desist orders from his father (Ted Levine), a tutor with clients in Anna's building.

Anna's family circle -- including her pregnant sister (Alison Elliot), husband Sean's best friend (Peter Stormare) and his secret-harboring wife (Anne Heche) -- respond with an understandably unsettled blend of bemusement and befuddlement, while the normally even-keeled Joseph becomes increasingly irritable about having to compete with a boy not yet out of grammar school.

Though strangely drawn to the child, Anna doesn't believe -- or won't let herself believe -- Sean's story, but when he begins to reveal intimate knowledge of their past life together, she begins to wonder if, as irrational as it sounds, he is telling the truth.
Kidman delivers a hypnotic performance, highlighted by a scene at an opera where a lingering close-up of Anna's face underscored by music from Wagner's Ring Cycle says more about her tender emotional state than any words could. Bright exudes an eerie blend of innocence and otherworldly gravitas, holding his own in scenes with Kidman. Bacall is at her imperious best and injects a bit of sardonic humor into the solemn-toned affair.

The cinematography by Harris Savides is appropriately moody, from its shadowy Gotham interiors, to its doleful wintry tableaus.

The film ends on a rather ambiguous note, never committing one way or the other to either a supernatural or psychological solution to the central mystery. And while contrary to the Catholic understanding of life after death, the theme of reincarnation is handled in an intelligent manner. Glazer wisely downplays the paranormal angle in favor of realism, making the implausible premise more believable.

As for the controversy surrounding "Birth," the film contains scenes which many viewers will find extremely troubling. They include one in an ice-cream parlor where Anna questions Sean about his sexual experience; another in which she kisses him chastely -- but longingly -- on the lips; and the much-talked-about scene in which Sean undresses before climbing into a bathtub with Anna.
While the scenes are not sexual in nature and seem to make sense within the context of the story, the narrative purpose of each could have been handled in any number of other less exploitative, equally effective ways. The bathroom scene (filmed with restraint over Kidman's bare shoulders) does not involve any nudity, but that may not be enough to dispel viewers' concerns that no amount of delicacy can justify such imagery.

Because of these scenes and one other explicit sexual encounter with nudity, the USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is O -- morally offensive. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted.
